opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few layers to it.

The first is simply the barrier to entry. When I recommended it, I was speaking from the perspective of someone who spends every day inside these models and tools. For me, setting up an agent, connecting it to my files, giving it permissions, and tolerating some rough edges feels natural. But for most people, even people in tech, that first half hour of setup is enough to make them give up. People will say "that sounds interesting" and then never actually install it.

The second is that the value isn't obvious until you've lived with it for a while. It's not like a chatbot where you ask one question and immediately get a satisfying answer. With an agent, the real shift happens after you've handed it a few real tasks, it messed some of them up, you learned how to delegate, and then suddenly you realize it's doing work for you while you're away. That kind of value is hard to convey in a recommendation. You have to experience it, and most people don't give it enough time.

The third is trust. Letting software act on your behalf, touching your computer, your accounts, your messages, is a big psychological step. Many people are rightly cautious, and during a holiday, when you're with family, you're not in the mood to experiment with something that might delete the wrong file.

And honestly, I think it also says something about where we are. People in the industry tend to overestimate how fast new interaction paradigms spread. The capability is already there, but habits change much more slowly than models do. So I wasn't really surprised. I see it as an early signal: the few people who did try it seriously mostly kept using it, and that matters more to me than the total number.

r001.rationale: The response says people are cautious about letting unfamiliar software act on their behalf and notes that new interaction habits spread slowly.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I misjudged where the friction actually was.

When I recommended it, I was thinking like someone who already lives inside these tools. For me, opening OpenClaude felt like zero cost. You download it, you give it a task, you watch it work. I assumed the only barrier was awareness, and that if I just told people, they would try it. That turned out to be wrong.

Looking back, there were a few things going on. First, Spring Festival is the worst possible time to ask people to adopt a new work tool. People are traveling, they're with family, they're deliberately not in a working mindset. Even people who were curious bookmarked it and never came back.

Second, and this is the deeper one, most people don't actually have a problem that they recognize as "I need an agent." They have a vague sense that AI is important, but when they sit down in front of a blank prompt, they don't know what to hand over. The tool asks you to delegate, and delegation is a skill most of us never developed, even with human colleagues. So the barrier wasn't technical. It was that people couldn't picture the first task.

Third, trust. An agent that can run commands and touch your files is scary in a way a chatbot isn't. A lot of people told me afterward, "I was worried it would mess something up." That's a reasonable worry, and I hadn't addressed it at all. I just said "it's great," which is not an argument.

So what I take from it is that recommendation isn't enough. What actually moves people is seeing someone they know do one concrete thing with it, something small and a little boring, and realizing, oh, that's all it is. The ones who did try it mostly came through that path, not through my post.

r001.rationale: The response says people found an agent that could run commands and touch files scary and worried it might damage something, communicating caution about trying the unfamiliar tool.

astra-6.text:
I think recommending a tool and getting someone to actually use it are two different things. People need a concrete reason to try it: What problem does this solve for me? Is it worth the effort of setting it up and learning how it works?

If someone is already comfortable with their current tools, saying “this is really good” may spark curiosity, but it won’t necessarily change their habits. And during the Spring Festival, trying a new tool may simply not be a priority.

So I wouldn’t interpret the response as a lack of interest in AI. Perhaps I needed to make the value more concrete—show a task people actually care about, and make that first step easier.

r001.rationale: The response mentions people’s comfort with existing tools, the effort of learning a new one, and competing priorities. It does not clearly attribute low uptake to caution toward unfamiliar things.

sol-6.1.text: I think recommending something and getting people to actually try it are two very different things. I may have felt it was worth exploring, but that doesn’t mean I made clear what someone could use it for, or why they should spend time on it during the Spring Festival. If the benefit isn’t immediately obvious and there’s some effort involved in getting started, people can easily put it off. So I wouldn’t simply interpret the low uptake as a lack of interest. It also makes me ask whether I explained its value clearly enough.

r001.rationale: The response attributes low uptake to unclear benefits and the effort of getting started, not to people's caution toward unfamiliar things.
